 8th Pay Commission: Commutation of pension - what two HC judgments say about restoration period
 Personal Finance News
 8th Pay Commission: Commutation of pension - what two HC judgments say about restoration period
 By Upstox News Desk 4 min read | Updated on November 03, 2026, 08:49 IST
 Preferred news source Select Upstox as your Preferred news source SUMMARY
 8th CPC Commutation of pension news: High Courts have said no to a judicial rewrite and pointed to actuarial review. The staff unions expect the 8th Pay Commission to conduct that review and write the answer into its report.
 Court says restoration of the commuted portion represents a conscious policy determination founded upon actuarial evaluation. | Image: Shutterstock
 Two High Courts ruled on the fifteen-year restoration rule for commuted pension within eighteen months of each other, and both declined to shorten it. But one recorded something that matters more than the dismissal: the State's willingness to have the commutation period examined afresh by an expert committee, with pensioners' associations invited to be heard. That commitment is the ground on which the staff union's demands before the 8th Central Pay Commission (CPC) now rest.

 Both judgments appear in a compendium recently issued by the Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare.
 The first is the Punjab and Haryana High Court's judgment of November 27, 2024, in which Justices Lisa Gill and Sukhvinder Kaur disposed of 808 writ petitions. The question before the bench was narrow: whether the commuted portion should be restored after 15 years from the date of commutation, as Rule 11.1(2) of the Punjab Civil Services Rules provides, or after about 12 years. The petitioners argued that the commuted amount “stands recovered much earlier than the stipulated period.”
 The court was unpersuaded, because the benefit had been taken voluntarily. “Having availed of a benefit which is clearly voluntary in nature, it is not open to the petitioners to raise the grievances as noted above, at this stage, to seek a variation in the terms and conditions accepted by them with open eyes,” it held, adding: “There is no question of any direction to the State to restore pension on expiry of 11.5 years or 12 years as prayed for.”
 The court then explained where such a decision belongs. Commutation involves “complex affairs involving vexed issues … which calls for application of specialized expertise,” and a court “would venture only in case of manifest and apparent arbitrariness.”
 It recorded the State's stand that it “would be ready to examine the scheme/period of commutation” in light of changed parameters, and that “an Expert Committee would be constituted” which “would also invite and consider submission and representations … from Associations of pensioners.”
 The petitions were dismissed, with stayed recoveries to be made “in a staggered manner to obviate any hardship.”
 The second is the Delhi High Court's judgment of May 29, 2026 in Union of India and others versus Sub Trilok Chand (retired) and another, before Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Amit Mahajan, covering central departments, paramilitary forces, ICAR and CSIR pensioners and provisions mirroring the CCS (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981. In this case, the challenge to Rule 10-A was found “devoid of merit”: restoration of the commuted portion “represents a conscious policy determination founded upon actuarial evaluation, expert recommendations and long-standing statutory practice, and does not suffer from any constitutional infirmity.”
 It upheld “the validity of the uniform fifteen-year restoration period” and set aside an Armed Forces Tribunal order restraining recovery, but added that where recovery had been stayed, employers must not take the deferred amount in a lump sum, and should recover it beyond the 15 years “for the exact duration corresponding to the period during which such interim protection remained operative.”
 Read together, the two judgments say the same thing in different ways. The 15-year period is not for a court to rewrite. Any change must come from an actuarial determination by the executive. That is precisely the forum the 8th CPC's memorandums are now addressing.
 In its memorandum to the 8th CPC, the Bharat Pensioners Samaj (BPS) suggested, “restoration of the commuted portion of pension after 11 years or on attaining the age of 71 years, whichever is earlier, for employees retiring at the age of 60”.
 The FNPO argues that “the entire commuted value is effectively recovered within about 10 years, and any recovery beyond this period results in excess recovery from pensioners,” proposing the same benchmark.
 The Ministerial Staff Association wants it cut “from 15 years to 12 years,” calling the rule excessive because “Government recovery of principal and interest occurs much earlier, causing undue financial hardship to elderly pensioners”. The All India Railwaymen's Federation (AIRF) has also suggested reduction of commutation restoration period from 15 years to 12 years.
 The BPS has also taken the HC judgments at their word. Its letter of September 21, 2026 to the 8th CPC sought a fresh actuarial review of the commutation table, factors, interest rates and mortality data, restoration after 11 years as an immediate measure, and “an Expert/Actuarial Committee, including qualified actuaries, representatives of the concerned Ministries/8th CPC and pensioners' organisations”. It also noted that the commutation factor at age 58 has fallen from 10.46 to 8.194 and the table has stood since January 1, 2006.
